I would not frame it as “stupid.” A more useful explanation is that presidents often appear unintelligent to critics for four main reasons.
First, many presidential decisions are politically strategic rather than intellectually elegant. A choice can seem irrational from a policy perspective while still being aimed at energizing supporters, dominating media coverage, or forcing institutions and opponents to react. That can make a president look reckless or simplistic even when the behavior is deliberate. Recent White House releases, for example, show an aggressively assertive style on foreign policy and tariffs, which supporters present as strength and critics often read as impulsiveness or poor judgment.

Second, the presidency rewards message discipline more than nuance. Public communication is usually compressed into slogans, applause lines, and adversarial contrasts. That style often sounds intellectually thin, especially to people who value careful reasoning, technical detail, or consistency. A president may therefore sound “dumb” not because he lacks basic intelligence, but because mass politics rewards bluntness.
Third, people often infer intelligence from whether they agree with outcomes. When a president backs policies you consider harmful, incoherent, or morally objectionable, it is natural to interpret that as stupidity. But the underlying problem may instead be ideology, incentives, misinformation, overconfidence, or indifference to consequences.
Fourth, modern presidents govern through a dense media environment in which every contradiction, exaggeration, and verbal misstep is amplified. That creates a constant stream of evidence for opponents who already see the president as unfit, while supporters interpret the same behavior differently.
So the sharper claim is usually not that the president is unintelligent, but that he may be acting with poor judgment, weak regard for evidence, strong ideological bias, or high tolerance for chaos. Those are analytically clearer criticisms than “stupid.”
